entities.name: Thomas Cranmer
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thomas Cranmer (1489–1556) was the first Protestant Archbishop of Canterbury and the principal architect of the Church of England's theological and liturgical identity. Born in Nottinghamshire, he rose through Cambridge scholarship to royal favour, and Henry VIII appointed him Archbishop in 1533, enabling the king's annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and England's break with Rome.

Cranmer's most enduring achievement was the Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised 1552), which he crafted in luminous English prose that shaped the language of Protestant worship for five centuries. His 42 Articles (later 39) established Anglican doctrinal foundations. He oversaw the English Reformation's legislative programme through the reigns of Henry VIII and Edward VI, systematically dismantling medieval Catholic practice — dissolving chantries, reforming canon law, and vernacularising the Mass.

Under the Catholic Queen Mary I, Cranmer was arrested for heresy and treason. After a long imprisonment he recanted his Protestantism multiple times under pressure, but at his execution in 1556 he dramatically withdrew all recantations and thrust his right hand — the hand that had signed the recantations — first into the flames, dying with the memorable cry 'this hand hath offended.' His martyrdom became foundational to English Protestant identity, immortalised in Foxe's Book of Martyrs.
